expect: Two defects at once, and both are the 'served as HTML' class. The document declares XHTML 1.0 Transitional (XML rules: every element closed, attributes quoted) but is delivered as text/html, so an XML parser must not be used on it. Separately the transport declares charset=UTF-8 while the bytes are not decodable as UTF-8 — a strict decode raises, and the crawler must fall back rather than drop the page.
evidence: measured 2026-07-26 (two fetches, identical counts both times) by feeding the live body to BOTH lxml.etree.HTMLParser(recover=True) — quoting its error_log verbatim — and a html.parser tag-balance walk that separates optional-end unclosed tags from genuinely mismatched nesting: HTTP 200, 34,787 bytes, content-type 'text/html; charset=UTF-8', DOCTYPE 'html PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD XHTML 1.0 Transitional//EN" "http://www.w3.org/TR/xhtml1/DTD/xhtml1-transitional.dtd"'. bytes.decode('utf-8') RAISES UnicodeDecodeError even though the header promises UTF-8 (2 non-ASCII bytes, neither of them a valid UTF-8 sequence). lxml's HTML parser reported 0 errors — proof that 'the HTML parser is happy' is not the same as 'the document is well-formed'; the tag-balance walk still found 1 mismatched <div>, and the XHTML document carries 29 <font> tags, which XHTML 1.0 Transitional permits but XHTML Strict does not.
defect: XHTML 1.0 Transitional served as text/html; body is NOT valid UTF-8 despite charset=UTF-8

expect: The original 1996 Space Jam site, preserved. No DOCTYPE means quirks-mode parsing, and the unescaped ampersands are the common real-world entity defect: '&' followed by text that is not a valid entity name. A parser that errors on a bad entity reference instead of emitting a literal '&' loses the URLs those ampersands sit inside.

expect: The two encoding declarations directly contradict each other. Per spec the transport header wins, but plenty of parsers prefer the meta, so the same bytes decode two different ways depending on which the crawler believes. This row exists to pin the precedence rule down rather than leave it to whichever library is in the path.
evidence:

expect: The XML-served-where-HTML-is-expected case. The crawler's harness passes any body whose content-type contains 'xml' to the same diagnose()/visible_text() path as HTML, so an XML document does get run through HTML machinery. Every RSS element is unknown to the HTML parser and <link> is void in HTML but has content in RSS, so </link> reads as a stray end tag on every single item. It must degrade to 'unknown tags, still readable text', not to an exception.
